newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission meets on draft energy tax directive.
newsitem.headline: Commission meets on draft energy tax directive.

text.p: The European Commission was expected to adopt a draft directive on Wednesday to raise the minimum taxes on motor and heating fuels later and extend the taxes to electricity and natural gas.
"I'm optimistic it will go through," said a senior aide to commissioner Mario Monti who is in charge of the EU's single market and taxation.
Fiercely opposed by industry, particularly heavy energy users like transport firms, and by some in the Commission itself, the controversial proposal was delayed twice in February.

But it looks set to go through this time after successive amendments to the text aimed at lessening the tax increases and urging national governments to use any additional revenue to cut non-wage labour costs, like social security payments.
The proposal was called for by EU governments themselves to compensate for the failure to agree a carbondioxide tax in the early 1990's to cut harmful emissions.
The draft directive on the taxation of energy products sets a minimum tax on motor diesel of 310 European currency units ($352) per 1,000 litres from January 1, 1998 from a current 245 Ecus.
The actual rates in the EU's 15 states are already above the proposed new minimum, except in Greece (252 Ecus), Luxembourg (262 Ecus), Spain (267 Ecus) and Austria (294 Ecus).
In the case of petrol, for which Monti's services propose a minimum level of 417 Ecus, even fewer countries would be affected. But the industry argues that the proposal sets the wrong trend.

"By the time the directive comes into force it will pose no problem, but even so it's about harmonising upwards," an oil industry source said. The plan foresees further tax increases in 2000 and 2002.

Inside the 20-member Commission, the proposal has run into opposition, although on different economic grounds, from Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann, Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan and Economic Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy.

But others, notably energy chief Christos Papoutsis and the two Spanish commissioners Manuel Marin and Marcelino Oreja have also raised reservations. The Spanish commissioners fear the tax could lead to another damaging lorry strike in Spain, similar to that of earlier this year.

Monti will need to get 10 commissioners to back him to push the proposal through but even then the issue will be far from settled. The draft directive will then go to EU finance ministers who must agree unanimously before it can become law.
The text which was on the table last week also foresees the introduction of an minimum tax on electricity of one Ecu per megawatt-hour in 1998. This would rise to two and three Ecus in 2000 and 2002.
Industry and Commission officials said the proposed rates had not changed.
Natural gas would also be taxed 2.9 Ecus per gigajoule in 1998 when used as a motor fuel and 0.2 Ecus for heating purposes. This is opposed by producing countries the Netherlands and Britain.
